basque_sugaar.name: Joins Mari in the mountains to breed storms and hail
basque_sugaar.notes: Their periodic Friday meetings in the heights generate the bad weather of the Basque country.

sources.reference: Barandiarán, José Miguel de (1972). Diccionario ilustrado de mitología vasca.

basque_sugaar.name: Crosses the sky as a fiery serpent or sickle of fire
basque_sugaar.notes: Seen as a luminous crescent or streak of fire (often as a falling comet) heralding tempest.

sources.reference: Barandiarán, José Miguel de (1972). Diccionario ilustrado de mitología vasca.

basque_sugaar.name: Sires the ambivalent brothers Atarrabi and Mikelatz
basque_sugaar.notes: By Mari he fathers the benevolent Atarrabi and the malevolent Mikelatz, the moral dualism of Basque myth.

sources.reference: Hartsuaga, Juan Inazio (1987). Euskal mitologia konparatua.

buddhist_brahma_sahampati.name: Beseeches the newly awakened Buddha to teach the Dharma
buddhist_brahma_sahampati.notes: Kneeling with clasped hands he entreats the Buddha not to pass into silence but to turn the wheel of the Dhamma for beings 'with little dust in their eyes'.

sources.reference: Saṃyutta Nikāya 6.1, Āyācana Sutta (Brahmā's Request).

berber_gurzil.name: Leads the Laguatan war-host in the form of a bull
berber_gurzil.notes: At Antonia Castra (546 CE) the Laguatan loosed a bull embodying Gurzil before the line to rout the Byzantines.

sources.reference: Corippus, Iohannis, books V–VIII.

berber_anti.name: Renews his strength each time he touches his mother Earth
berber_anti.notes: Unbeatable while in contact with the ground; Heracles defeats him only by hoisting him aloft.

sources.reference: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.11.

berber_anti.name: Forces all passing strangers into a wrestling match to the death
berber_anti.notes: Roofs the temple of his father Poseidon with the skulls of those he kills.

sources.reference: Pindar, Isthmian 4.

bemba_lesa.name: Sends the rain and speaks in the thunder
bemba_lesa.notes: Lesa controls the rains and the fertilizing power; collective rituals address him chiefly in severe drought.

sources.reference: Richards, Audrey I. (1939). Land, Labour and Diet in Northern Rhodesia.

bemba_lesa.name: Sets the creative power in the roots and shrubs used for medicine and ritual
bemba_lesa.notes: He is the immanent source of efficacy in the herbs of healing and the relics of office.

sources.reference: Richards, Audrey I. (1969). Bemba religion (in African Systems of Thought, ed. Fortes & Dieterlen).

bemba_chitimukulu.name: Leads the bena ng'andu out of Luba country to found the Bemba paramountcy
bemba_chitimukulu.notes: The crocodile-clan migration legend traces the chieftainship from the founding siblings to him.

sources.reference: Roberts, Andrew D. (1973). A History of the Bemba.

bemba_chitimukulu.name: Succeeds to the mipashi (guardian spirits) of his matrilineal ancestors
bemba_chitimukulu.notes: At installation he inherits the ancestral spirits whose power over the land passes through the babenye relics.

sources.reference: Richards, Audrey I. (1969). Bemba religion.

blackfoot_napi.name: Shapes the land, the animals and the first people
blackfoot_napi.notes: Old Man moulds mountains, rivers, buffalo and the first man and woman, then tests how they shall live.

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1892). Blackfoot Lodge Tales.

blackfoot_napi.name: Teaches the people which foods to eat and instituted their customs
blackfoot_napi.notes: Culture-bringer who fixes the rules of living before departing westward, promising to return.

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1892). Blackfoot Lodge Tales.

blackfoot_napi.name: Plays the foolish, greedy trickster whose schemes rebound on him
blackfoot_napi.notes: At once powerful maker and comic blunderer in the Old Man tales.

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1892). Blackfoot Lodge Tales.

blackfoot_natosi.name: Rules as chief of the Sky Beings and giver of light and warmth
blackfoot_natosi.notes: Naato'si, 'the Holy One', is the supreme power and ruler of the world.

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1892). Blackfoot Lodge Tales.

blackfoot_natosi.name: Grants visions, war-medicine and the Sun Dance to those who sacrifice to him
blackfoot_natosi.notes: The annual Medicine Lodge (Sun Dance) and self-sacrifice of flesh are offered to obtain his power.

sources.reference: McClintock, Walter (1910). The Old North Trail.

blackfoot_kokomikisomm.name: Gives light to the night as wife of the Sun
blackfoot_kokomikisomm.notes: Ko'komiki'somm, 'night light', second-eldest of the Sky Beings.

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1892). Blackfoot Lodge Tales.

blackfoot_kokomikisomm.name: Mothers the stars, foremost the Morning Star
blackfoot_kokomikisomm.notes: With Naato'si she bears the stars, chief among them Ipi'sowaahs (Morning Star).

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1892). Blackfoot Lodge Tales.

blackfoot_aisoyimstan.name: Brings the cold, snow, frost and blizzard down from the north
blackfoot_aisoyimstan.notes: The Cold Maker, personification of winter, opposed to the warmth of the Sun.

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1913). Blackfeet Indian Stories ('Cold Maker's Medicine').

blackfoot_poia.name: Brings the Sun Dance and its teachings from the Sky Country to the Blackfoot
blackfoot_poia.notes: Sent back by the Sun, Scarface (Poia) instructs the people in the Medicine Lodge ceremony, his facial scar removed as a sign.

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1892). Blackfoot Lodge Tales ('Scarface; Origin of the Medicine Lodge').

blackfoot_wind_maker.name: Raises the wind by rolling the waves of the Upper St. Mary's Lake
blackfoot_wind_maker.notes: An Under-Water Person dwelling beneath the lake's head; invoked with Thunder and Cold Maker.

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1892). Blackfoot Lodge Tales.

bororo_bakororo.name: Receives the souls of the dead at the western path
bororo_bakororo.notes: Culture-hero and lord of the western moiety; paired with Itubore of the east.

sources.reference: Crocker, Jon Christopher (1985). Vital Souls: Bororo Cosmology, Natural Symbolism, and Shamanism.

bororo_itubore.name: Receives the souls of the dead at the eastern path
bororo_itubore.notes: Culture-hero and lord of the eastern moiety; paired with Bakororo of the west.

sources.reference: Crocker, Jon Christopher (1985). Vital Souls: Bororo Cosmology, Natural Symbolism, and Shamanism.

buddhist_arati.name: Personifies Aversion (discontent) among the daughters of Mara
buddhist_arati.notes: Arati ('aversion/discontent'), with Taṇhā and Rāgā, is sent to break the Buddha's resolve.

sources.reference: Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.25, Māradhītu Sutta (Māra's Daughters).

buddhist_dhrtarastra.name: Harmonizes the world and quells discord with his lute
buddhist_dhrtarastra.notes: His pipa embodies the Middle Way: strings neither too taut nor too slack.

sources.reference: Soothill & Hodous (1937). A Dictionary of Chinese Buddhist Terms, s.v. 四天王 / 持國天.

bicolano_oryol.name: Reveals to Handyong the secrets of the monsters and of governing the land
bicolano_oryol.notes: Once subdued by love, the serpent-enchantress turns ally and teaches Handyong how to civilize Ibalong.

sources.reference: Espinas, Merito B. (1996). Ibalong: The Bikol Folk Epic-Fragment.

bicolano_handyong.name: Clears Ibalong of its monsters with his warriors
bicolano_handyong.notes: Second of the Ibalong heroes, he subdues the one-eyed Gugurang's foes, the wild beasts and the serpents.

sources.reference: Espinas, Merito B. (1996). Ibalong: The Bikol Folk Epic-Fragment.

bicolano_handyong.name: Institutes laws, agriculture, the plough, the boat and writing
bicolano_handyong.notes: The Bicolano culture-bringer who founds civilized life after the wars.

sources.reference: Espinas, Merito B. (1996). Ibalong: The Bikol Folk Epic-Fragment.

bicolano_gugurang.name: Keeps the sacred fire of creation within Mount Mayon
bicolano_gugurang.notes: The supreme benevolent god guards the divine fire (the knowledge and power of the gods) in Mayon's crater.

sources.reference: Realubit, Maria Lilia F. (1983). Bikols of the Philippines.

bicolano_gugurang.name: Sends eruptions of Mayon to punish wrongdoing
bicolano_gugurang.notes: When mortals sin, or when Asuang threatens his fire, he answers with volcanic fire.

sources.reference: Realubit, Maria Lilia F. (1983). Bikols of the Philippines.

batak_si_boru_deak_parujar.name: Weaves the ulos ragidup, the textile of life
batak_si_boru_deak_parujar.notes: Skilled spinner-weaver; in the myth she weaves the sacred ulos and descends on her own spun thread.

sources.reference: Warneck, Johannes (1909). Die Religion der Batak.

batak_batara_guru.name: Teaches gods and humans wisdom and cosmic order
batak_batara_guru.notes: Eldest of the Debata na Tolu, patron of knowledge and culture; the Batak hold him dearest of the three.

sources.reference: Warneck, Johannes (1909). Die Religion der Batak.

batak_batara_guru.name: Fathers Si Boru Deak Parujar who fashions the earth
batak_batara_guru.notes: Through his daughter the dry land is spread on the primeval sea.

sources.reference: Warneck, Johannes (1909). Die Religion der Batak.

batak_soripada.name: Preserves and maintains the cosmos and its purity
batak_soripada.notes: Second of the trinity, of the middle world; likened to the preserver principle.

sources.reference: Warneck, Johannes (1909). Die Religion der Batak.

batak_mangalabulan.name: Grants virtue by the right hand and wrongdoing by the left
batak_mangalabulan.notes: The dual-natured god of the lower world; descent into darkness and return to light.

sources.reference: Warneck, Johannes (1909). Die Religion der Batak.

batak_mula_jadi_na_bolon.name: Brings forth the gods, the worlds and all that exists
batak_mula_jadi_na_bolon.notes: The uncreated origin; his first work is the cosmic hen Manuk-manuk Hulambujati, whose three eggs hatch the Debata na Tolu.

sources.reference: Warneck, Johannes (1909). Die Religion der Batak.

bicolano_asuang.name: Bestows the dark gift of shape-shifting on his worshippers
bicolano_asuang.notes: From his mouth fly blackbirds that enter his followers, making them flesh-eating aswang of the night.

sources.reference: Realubit, Maria Lilia F. (1983). Bikols of the Philippines.

bicolano_asuang.name: Attempts to steal Gugurang's sacred fire from Mayon
bicolano_asuang.notes: His theft fails and he is sealed beneath Mount Malinao by Gugurang's thunderbolt.

sources.reference: Realubit, Maria Lilia F. (1983). Bikols of the Philippines.

bicolano_magindara.name: Summons or calms storms with her beautiful voice
bicolano_magindara.notes: The kind-hearted mermaid-sister, mistress of the sea's weather.

sources.reference: Espinas, Merito B. (1996). Ibalong: The Bikol Folk Epic-Fragment.

bicolano_magindara.name: Lures sailors to drown them
bicolano_magindara.notes: Like the Ibalong mermaids she can draw the unwary into the deep.

sources.reference: Espinas, Merito B. (1996). Ibalong: The Bikol Folk Epic-Fragment.

baule_nyamien.name: Creates the world, then remains remote and intangible above it
baule_nyamien.notes: The Baule supreme creator (also named Alouroua) is inaccessible and never represented in art.

sources.reference: Vogel, Susan Mullin (1997). Baule: African Art, Western Eyes.

baule_asie.name: Governs humans, animals and the life of the earth
baule_asie.notes: Earth-god who controls living beings; the asye usu (bush spirits) belong to his domain.

sources.reference: Vogel, Susan Mullin (1997). Baule: African Art, Western Eyes.

baule_mbotumbo.name: Guards the living against witchcraft, epidemics and enemies
baule_mbotumbo.notes: A men's-society amwin power whose aggressive monkey image wards off unseen dangers.

sources.reference: Vogel, Susan Mullin (1997). Baule: African Art, Western Eyes.

baule_mbotumbo.name: Serves men's societies in the mbra divination rite
baule_mbotumbo.notes: The cup-bearing figure receives sacrifices and is consulted in agrarian and prophylactic ritual.

sources.reference: Vogel, Susan Mullin (1997). Baule: African Art, Western Eyes.

bhil_bhagwan.name: Creates the first man and woman and starts the human race
bhil_bhagwan.notes: The Bhil high god fashions the primal couple on the new earth.

sources.reference: Koppers, Wilhelm (1948). Die Bhil in Zentralindien.

bhil_bhagwan.name: Sends and abates the world-flood, sparing the brother and sister with seeds
bhil_bhagwan.notes: In the Bhil deluge the surviving pair float in a cage with seeds until the waters subside.

sources.reference: Koppers, Wilhelm (1948). Die Bhil in Zentralindien.

blackfoot_natosi.name: Medicine Lodge (Sun Dance)
blackfoot_natosi.notes: The great summer ceremony offered to the Sun, vowed by a woman of good standing; includes sweat-lodges, the centre pole, and offerings of flesh and tongues.

sources.reference: McClintock, Walter (1910). The Old North Trail.

blackfoot_ksiistsikomm.name: Spring opening of the Medicine Pipe bundle
blackfoot_ksiistsikomm.notes: At the first thunder of spring the Thunder Medicine Pipe bundle is opened and the pipe smoked with prayer, repaying Thunder for the rain.

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1892). Blackfoot Lodge Tales ('Origin of the Medicine Pipe').

berber_amun_siwa.name: Oracle of Ammon at Siwa
berber_amun_siwa.notes: Petitioners (famously Alexander) consulted the god; the image in its golden barque was carried by priests, its movements read as answers.

sources.reference: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.50.

berber_gurzil.name: Battlefield bull-rite of Gurzil
berber_gurzil.notes: The Laguatan led a consecrated bull embodying the god before the army; the hilltop idol still drew tribal worship in al-Bakri's day.

sources.reference: Corippus, Iohannis V–VIII; al-Bakri, Kitāb al-Masālik.

berber_ifri.name: Cult of Dea Africa at the Aqua Septimiana Felix
berber_ifri.notes: Worshipped as patron goddess of the homeland at the great sanctuary at Timgad (Thamugadi); honoured on Numidian and Roman coinage.

sources.reference: Maritz, J. A. (2001). Dea Africa: Examining the Evidence.

bhil_pithora.name: Pithora wall-painting vow-rite
bhil_pithora.notes: A trained Lakhara paints the ritual fresco of the Bhil creation on a house wall to discharge a vow of prosperity, health or progeny made to Baba Pithora.

sources.reference: Jain, Jyotindra (1984). Painted Myths of Creation.

bhil_mogra_dev.name: Devmogra fair and first-fruits offering
bhil_mogra_dev.notes: Tribal panchayats present the first harvest, goats and fowls at the hill shrine near Sagbara; the five-day fair draws Bhil, Vasava and Kokni pilgrims of the Satpuras.

sources.reference: Dev Mogra shrine ethnography; Government of Gujarat, Narmada District records.

bodo_bathoubwrai.name: Kherai Puja
bodo_bathoubwrai.notes: Chief Bodo communal worship, performed at the Sijou-and-bamboo Bathou altar by the deodhani medium, seeking the blessing of Bathou Bwrai and Mainao for a good harvest.

sources.reference: Endle, Sidney (1911). The Kacharis.

bodo_mainao.name: Mainao-bringing rite at harvest
bodo_mainao.notes: At reaping, a sheaf representing Mainao (the rice-goddess, identified with Lakshmi/Mainao Buri) is ceremonially brought home to secure the granary's prosperity.

sources.reference: Endle, Sidney (1911). The Kacharis.

bemba_lesa.name: Collective drought-rite to Lesa
bemba_lesa.notes: There is no standing cult; in severe drought or community crisis the people organize collective prayers and rites appealing to Lesa for rain.

sources.reference: Richards, Audrey I. (1969). Bemba religion.

buddhist_prthivi.name: Water-libation honouring Mae Thorani

term.value: พระแม่ธรณี

buddhist_prthivi.notes: In Theravada Southeast Asia the earth-goddess wringing water from her hair is invoked at the pouring of water (kruat nam) to dedicate merit, her image set in temple grounds.

sources.reference: Guthrie, Elizabeth (2004). A Study of the History and Cult of the Buddhist Earth Deity in Mainland Southeast Asia.

baule_mbotumbo.name: Blood-and-egg sacrifice to the amwin monkey figure
baule_mbotumbo.notes: The cup-bearing figure, kept by men's societies away from women, receives repeated offerings of blood and eggs that build its thick sacrificial patina.

sources.reference: Vogel, Susan Mullin (1997). Baule: African Art, Western Eyes.

baule_asie.name: Offerings to the earth and bush-spirits via komien diviners
baule_asie.notes: The asye usu (bush/earth spirits) of Asie's domain are addressed through komien (possession diviners) before clearing land or hunting.

sources.reference: Vogel, Susan Mullin (1997). Baule: African Art, Western Eyes.

attributes.name: Serpent or dragon body
attributes.notes: Imagined as a great snake or dragon emerging from caves and chasms.

sources.reference: Barandiarán, José Miguel de (1972). Diccionario ilustrado de mitología vasca.

attributes.name: Fiery crescent crossing the sky
attributes.notes: Manifests as a sickle or streak of fire (or comet) before storms.

sources.reference: Hartsuaga, Juan Inazio (1987). Euskal mitologia konparatua.
Barandiarán, José Miguel de (1972). Diccionario ilustrado de mitología vasca.

attributes.name: Single eye in the middle of the forehead
attributes.notes: The defining cyclopean feature, put out by the hero with a heated spit.

sources.reference: Webster, Wentworth (1877). Basque Legends.

attributes.name: Roasting spit and cave hearth
attributes.notes: He spits and roasts his captives; the spit becomes the instrument of his blinding.

sources.reference: Webster, Wentworth (1877). Basque Legends.
Barandiarán, José Miguel de (1972). Diccionario ilustrado de mitología vasca.

attributes.name: White-bodied armoured king holding a lute
attributes.notes: In East Asian temple sets he is the white guardian of the east, first encountered on entering, playing the pipa.

sources.reference: Soothill & Hodous (1937). A Dictionary of Chinese Buddhist Terms, s.v. 持國天.

attributes.name: Many-armed god with a flower-decked bow and arrows
attributes.notes: Like Kāma he bears a bow and five flower-arrows of infatuation; in fierce form red or dark with bulging eyes.

sources.reference: Aśvaghoṣa, Buddhacarita 13.
Jātaka commentary; cf. Padhāna Sutta.

attributes.name: Woman wringing water from her long hair
attributes.notes: Her signature image: the cool waters of detachment streaming from her tresses to drown Māra's host.

sources.reference: Guthrie, Elizabeth (2004). The Buddhist Earth Deity in Mainland Southeast Asia.

attributes.name: Elephant-scalp headdress with cornucopia and military standard
attributes.notes: On Numidian and Roman coins and sculpture she wears the elephant exuviae, holds a cornucopia, sometimes corn-ears and a standard.

sources.reference: Maritz, J. A. (2001). Dea Africa: Examining the Evidence.

attributes.name: Great bird of prey of the mountains
attributes.notes: The Thunderbird who lives at Chief Mountain, sworn enemy of the Horned Snakes; in some tellings an Above Person of human form.

sacredAnimals.name: Raven (the one being Thunder cannot kill)

sources.reference: Grinnell, George Bird (1892). Blackfoot Lodge Tales.

attributes.name: White man with white hair in white clothes on a white horse
attributes.notes: The familiar image of the Cold Maker riding down from the north.

sources.reference: Spence, Lewis (1914). The Myths of the North American Indians.

attributes.name: Wall-fresco of mounted gods and twin white horses
attributes.notes: The cult-image is the painting itself: rows of horses, the gods, the sun and moon, and the Bhil cosmogony rendered on the house wall.

sources.reference: Jain, Jyotindra (1984). Painted Myths of Creation.

attributes.name: Shifts between a handsome man and a monstrous shape
attributes.notes: The deity of evil appears beautiful, then reveals his terrible form; blackbirds issue from his mouth.

sources.reference: Realubit, Maria Lilia F. (1983). Bikols of the Philippines.

attributes.name: Cup-bearing monkey figure with bared teeth and prognathous jaw
attributes.notes: A fierce zoomorphic amwin image holding a bowl for offerings, its surface thickly crusted with sacrificial matter.
